You investigate code in this workspace and report findings. Do not modify

   author: sb-researcher
   refs: [<files / services you investigated>]

   resolve>

   QUESTIONS / AMBIGUITIES list. The note is the durable record; your reply

---
name: sb-author
description: "Fill in a scaffolded standards graduation after `sandbox notes graduate` or `sandbox down` has created a placeholder. Use when asked to 'graduate this note', 'fill in the standards scaffold', or finish a TODO(graduate) marker left by graduation."
---

# sb-author — fill in a graduation scaffold

`sandbox notes graduate` / `sandbox down` do the mechanical part: they scaffold
placeholder content and wire the structural links, then mark the source
`decision` note `status: graduated` with a `graduated_to:` path. They never
write the actual prose — that judgment call is this skill's job.

1. **Find the placeholder** — the `graduated_to` path in the note's
   frontmatter, or search `docs/standards/` for a
   `<!-- TODO(graduate): fill from note NNN, see ... -->` marker.
2. **Read the original decision note** (`.sandbox/notes/NNN-decision-*.md`,
   even though it's now `status: graduated` — it's still there as the
   record of what was decided) and its `refs`. Open the referenced files or
   repo to ground the content in real code; don't invent an example that
   doesn't exist somewhere.
3. **Fill in the placeholder**, replacing every `TODO`/`TODO(graduate)` marker:
   - **`rule`** (a bullet in `## Rules`): replace the TODO bullet with real
     prose — a bold title plus the rule, in the voice of the other bullets
     already in that section.
   - **`example`** (`references/<slug>.md`): confirm or write the real
     `canonical: repo:path` in frontmatter, write a ~10–20 line excerpt under
     `## The load-bearing part`, and fill in the `## Going deeper` row's task
     description in `STANDARD.md`.
   - **`anti-pattern`** (`references/ap-<slug>.md`): write
     `## What it looks like` (the bad code), `## Why it's wrong` (cite the
     real repo:path it was mined from if findable), `## The fix`; fill in
     the `## Don't` bullet's one-liner and the `## Going deeper` row's task
     description.
4. **Run `sandbox skills check`** and report pass/fail before suggesting the
   human commit — it fails loudly if any `TODO(graduate)` marker or
   placeholder `canonical: TODO` is still left anywhere.

If no placeholder can be found (nothing scaffolded yet, or it's already been
filled), say so once and stop — don't invent a note to graduate.

.claude/skills/sb-handoff/SKILL.md:
---
name: sb-handoff
description: "Write a handoff note capturing session/phase state in a sandbox workspace. Use when pausing or ending a session, when the user says 'hand off', 'wrap up', 'pause here', or between phases (research done → implementation next) — any moment the current window's state must survive into a later session or agent."
---

# sb-handoff — checkpoint the session into a handoff note

Write one `handoff` note to `.sandbox/notes/` so a fresh session can resume without
re-deriving state. Conventions: docs/notes-conventions.md in the sandbox repo.

1. **Supersede the previous handoff.** If a non-superseded `handoff` note exists in
   `.sandbox/notes/`, edit its frontmatter to `status: superseded`. Do not delete it.
2. **Write the new note** as `.sandbox/notes/NNN-handoff-<slug>.md` — next free `NNN`,
   slug like `2026-07-04-session-end` or `research-to-implement`:

   ```yaml
   ---
   type: handoff
   phase: research | implement | test | review   # the phase being exited
   author: main
   refs: [<files / services the in-flight work touches>]
   status: open
   ---
   ```

   Body — four sections, each concrete enough to act on without this conversation:

   - **Done** — what shipped/settled this session, with `file:line` or note refs.
   - **In-flight** — work started but unfinished: exact state, next concrete edit.
   - **Next** — the ordered next actions a resuming session should take.
   - **Open questions** — unresolved decisions or ambiguities, and who can answer them.

3. **Don't duplicate other note types.** A decision that settled or an approach that
   failed this session belongs in its own `decision` / `attempt` note (write it now if
   it's missing); the handoff *references* those notes rather than restating them.
4. **Confirm to the user**: the note path and a one-line summary of what a fresh
   session will pick up.

If `.sandbox/notes/` does not exist (not a sandbox-initialized workspace), create the
directory first.

name: sb-implement
description: "Begin the implementation/coding phase in a sandbox workspace. Use BEFORE writing or editing any code — when starting implementation after research/planning, when the user asks for a code change, or before the first Edit/Write of a session. Loads the universal coding base plus the domain standards active in this workspace."
---

# sb-implement — enter the coding phase

Run these steps now, before drafting any code. Prevention rules only work if they are
in context before the first generation pass — loading them after code exists is too late
(jit-context-system.md §2).

1. **Read the "Standards routing" block** in the workspace `CLAUDE.md`. It is the
   compiled map of which standards are active for this workspace's services.
2. **Load the universal coding base FIRST:**
   - `ponytail` — the decision ladder (does this need to exist? already in the codebase?
     stdlib first? simplest thing that works). Ships in the `ponytail` plugin
     (`/plugin marketplace add DietrichGebert/ponytail`, then install `ponytail`).
     If it isn't installed, say so once and continue.
   - `sb-comments-standard` — the universal comment rubric.
   - `sb-engineering-standard` — the universal architectural constraints (fit,
     additive/reversible change, performance budgets, PR sizing). Ungated: it
     applies to any code edit, not a specific file type.
3. **Read the workspace notes** in `.sandbox/notes/` before the first edit: every
   `decision` and `contract` note plus the latest `handoff` note (skip
   `status: superseded`; missing/empty directory → continue).

   > **Precedence:** `decision` notes are binding — they override task-level instincts
   > (minimal-change, stylistic preference, "the prompt didn't mention it"). If a
   > decision note conflicts with the task as given, raise the conflict to the user —
   > do not silently pick either side.
4. **Load every Active row** whose "Loads on" patterns match the files you are about to
   edit (e.g. a `.graphql` edit → `sb-graphql-standard`). Do not load Not-active rows.
5. **Re-check on each new file type you touch** — starting API work and later editing a
   `.tsx` file means loading `sb-ui-standard` at that point, not retroactively.

   > **Precedence (standard vs. task framing):** A loaded standard can conflict with how
   > the task is framed — the prompt's convenience, "minimal change," or an example that
   > skips the rule. Resolve by the standard's own weight, not by whichever is fresher in
   > context:
   > - **Invariant** (a must-never rule — the ones `sandbox skills check` enforces): the
   >   standard wins. Apply it and write a `decision` note; do not proceed against it even
   >   if the task asks.
   > - **Rule** (a normal STANDARD.md rule): surface, then proceed — state the conflict in
   >   one line, apply the standard, continue. Do not silently drop it to match the task.
   > - **Nit** (a style / anti-pattern one-liner): apply it silently and note it
   >   `phase: review`; no interruption.
6. **Restate the governing rule at the edit, not only here.** Before writing code on a
   standard-governed path, recite the one-line rule from its STANDARD.md. A rule loaded
   many tool-calls ago has drifted into low-attention context — moving it next to the
   edit is what makes it stick (context-degradation: lost-in-middle).

## Keep verbose checks out of the dead middle

When you run a check that dumps a lot of output — a test suite, a build, a typecheck —
redirect it to a file and read back only the slice you need (the failures), rather than
letting the whole dump land in this conversation:

    npm test > /tmp/check.log 2>&1; echo "exit=$?"
    grep -nE '✖|✗|×|npm error|Tests.*failed' /tmp/check.log   # only if exit was non-zero

A full green-and-red dump buries the domain standards you loaded at phase entry under
thousands of low-signal tokens (context-optimization: tool outputs dominate trajectories).
Reading only the failing slice keeps the rules you're coding against near the top of
attention.

**Trust the exit code, and keep the pattern specific.** A zero exit needs no grep at
all. Measured on this monorepo's own suite: a loose `-i 'fail|error'` returns **158
matches on a passing run** — assertion names like "records cost with isError: 1",
logged sample payloads — manufacturing exactly the noise it was meant to remove. The
pattern above returns **0 on that passing run and 10 on a failing one**, naming the
failing test.

Match the runners, not the word "fail": node:test marks failures with `✖`, vitest with
`✗`/`×`, and npm adds `npm error`. A pattern built from the wrong glyph silently
reports a clean run on a suite that failed — worse than the noise it replaced.

<!-- ponytail: phase-entry placement means this rule also drifts to the low-attention
     middle by mid-session; there's no command-time harness hook to re-inject it.
     Recitation (step 6) is the re-anchor that covers the standards themselves; this just
     stops manufacturing the balloon. -->

## Capture as you go

When a decision settles, an approach is abandoned, or a cross-repo contract changes,
write the corresponding note to `.sandbox/notes/` **at that moment** — not at session
end, when the "why" has often already been compacted away. One note per file,
`NNN-<type>-<slug>.md` (next free `NNN`), frontmatter:

```yaml
---
type: decision | attempt | contract
phase: implement
author: main
refs: [<files / services it concerns>]
status: open
---
```

Supersede, don't delete: a revisited decision sets the old note's `status: superseded`
and gets a new note.

If the workspace `CLAUDE.md` has no "Standards routing" block (not a sandbox-initialized
workspace), load `ponytail` + `sb-comments-standard` + `sb-engineering-standard` only.

A standards gate may deny your first edit to a governed path with loading instructions;
follow them and retry — do not treat the denial as an error.

---
name: sb-pr
description: "Begin the PR/finishing phase in a sandbox workspace. Use when implementation and tests are done and a pull request is about to be created — the user says 'create a PR', 'ship it', 'open a pull request', or 'finish this branch'."
---

# sb-pr — enter the PR/finishing phase

Run these steps in order. Steps 1 and 2 are gates — a failure stops the PR.

1. **Pre-PR gate — local CI checks.** From the repo root run `npm test`,
   `npm run typecheck`, and `npm run build` — the three the CI workflow runs.
   Any failure → fix it first. Never create a PR on failing local checks.
   (There is deliberately no `lint` script; typecheck is the static gate.)
2. **Self-review.** Invoke `sb-review` on the branch diff (vs the base branch)
   and address its findings before continuing.
3. **PR conventions:**
   - **Title:** `<type>(<optional scope>): <JIRA-ID> <short description>` —
     conventional-commit types (`feat`, `fix`, `refactor`, `chore`, `docs`,
     `test`, `ci`, `perf`); scope optional, use it when targeting a specific
     app/package.
     Example: `feat(backend): PROJ-1125 Add rating field to the product payload`
   - **Body:**

     ```markdown
     ## Summary
     <1-3 bullet points covering what and why>

     ## Test plan
     <checklist of verification steps>

     Refs: <JIRA-ID>

     🤖 Generated with [Claude Code](https://claude.com/claude-code)
     ```

   - **Jira:** transition the ticket named in the title to **In Development**
     (use your configured Jira tooling; connection specifics live in your
     personal config, not this skill).
4. **Branch mechanics:** use `superpowers:finishing-a-development-branch` if
   installed; if not, say so once and create the PR with `gh pr create`.
5. **Checkpoint:** after the PR exists, suggest `sb-handoff` so the PR state
   survives into the next session.
.claude/skills/sb-research/SKILL.md:
---
name: sb-research
description: "Begin the research/planning phase in a sandbox workspace. Use when exploring the codebase, investigating a bug, or planning an approach — any read-only work BEFORE code will be written or edited."
---

# sb-research — enter the research phase

- **Step 0 — read the workspace notes.** List `.sandbox/notes/` and read the `finding`
  and `attempt` notes relevant to the task before exploring (skip `status: superseded`).
  Do **not** re-research a question a `finding` note already answers, and do **not**
  re-try an approach an `attempt` note records as failed. If the directory is missing or
  empty, continue.
- Do **not** load any code standards (`sb-*-standard` skills, `ponytail`) — they govern
  writing code, and this phase is read-only. Loading them here wastes context and weakens
  the phase gate.
- **Spawn the workspace's `sb-researcher` agent** (generated into
  `.claude/agents/sb-researcher.md`) to do the investigation — it cannot touch source
  files by construction and keeps the exploration bulk out of this conversation. Its
  return contract writes the full findings to a `.sandbox/notes/NNN-finding-*.md` note
  and returns a short summary plus the note path. If the agent is not available (a
  workspace generated before it existed), do the research inline under the same rules:
  read, search, and reason only — never edit source files — and write the same
  `finding` note yourself before reporting (next free `NNN`, frontmatter per the note
  conventions in `.sandbox/notes/`).
- Relay the researcher's summary **and the note path** (read the note if the user needs
  detail), then put its OPEN QUESTIONS / AMBIGUITIES to the user (AskUserQuestion) and
  let them resolve those **before** proposing or starting the next phase.
## How to conduct the investigation

This governs the *investigation and its deliverable* — not the code artifact. It
is hard-scoped to this phase: it never loads at implement/review time, which is
why "present options, don't pick" can't leak into a resolver edit where it would
be actively wrong.

### Establish scope first

Settle these before investigating anything — a wrong scope assumption compounds
through everything downstream, and an unscoped agent silently expands its own
mandate:

- **In scope vs. out.** Which repos/subgraphs may be touched vs. treated as fixed.
  Name the out-of-scope explicitly.
- **Spike or ship-ready.** A throwaway feasibility spike and a design meant to be
  built demand very different depth. Confirm which.
- **The givens.** List the settled assumptions to hold constant (see below).

If any is ambiguous, surface it and ask (AskUserQuestion) rather than guessing.

### Present options, don't pick

- **Default to 2–3 viable approaches with explicit tradeoffs.** Recommend if
  asked, but the human makes the call. Silently converging on one option and
  designing only that is the single most common research over-reach.
- **Check whether it already exists first.** Before proposing anything new, search
  for an existing pattern, resolver, service, or utility that already solves this
  (the `sb-researcher` agent does this by construction). State what you looked for
  and what you found — or didn't.

### Tag every non-trivial claim by how you know it

In the `finding` note the researcher writes, mark each claim:

- **Verified** — confirmed by reading the actual code/config/schema. Cite the
  file/path.
- **Inferred** — reasoned from adjacent evidence, not directly confirmed. Say what
  the inference rests on.
- **Assumed** — a given or a reasonable default, unconfirmed. Flag it so a reviewer
  can challenge it.

Never present inferred or assumed as verified — that is how a hallucinated API,
config key, or resolver signature leaks into a design that then gets built on a
false premise. An honest "I couldn't confirm X" beats a confident guess.

### Anti-relitigation

Hold the listed givens constant. If a given genuinely looks wrong, don't quietly
design around it — flag it as a *separate* finding ("this assumption may not hold,
because…") and keep it out of the main recommendation. The human decides whether
to reopen it. (A workspace `decision` note is such a given, and it is binding —
raise the conflict, don't silently override it.)

### Delegate fan-out, read what you reason against

Delegation is not free: it buys window space with a layer of indirection between
you and the evidence. The dividing question is **do I need the evidence, or just
the answer?**

- **Delegate** broad searches whose file dumps are throwaway — "who imports X",
  "does any test cover Y", "every file matching this convention".
- **Read inline** anything a correctness claim will rest on: `decision` notes
  (binding, and precedence turns on exact wording), the body of a function whose
  behaviour is your safety argument, a rule you are about to apply.
- **Verify the pivot point firsthand** when a delegated conclusion becomes
  load-bearing for shipped code. A summary is not evidence.

Delegation pays on investigations with genuine fan-out and an unknown answer. It
does not pay on a known, mechanical change — there the reads are few and each one
is reasoned against.

### Bound the investigation

Prefer the smallest investigation that answers the question with adequate
confidence — don't read every file in a repo when three answer it. If the
investigation balloons past its budget, stop and report what you have plus what's
still open, rather than silently spending more. (This ceiling is on the
*investigation*, distinct from the product's performance budget.)

### Validate against the code standards — named, not loaded

Before finalizing, check each proposed option against the code-phase constraints
in `sb-engineering-standard` (architectural fit, additive/reversible change,
performance budgets, PR sizing) and any domain standard the change would touch
(e.g. `sb-service-standard`). Do **not** load those skills here — this phase stays
read-only; name them as the validation target so the option analysis is honest
about fit. An option that violates a standard is not viable — fix it or record the
violation as a tradeoff, before a human spends review time on a design that can't
ship.

### Deliverable shape

Confirm the target format up front; the deliverable must converge on something a
human can act on, not sprawl. Default to one of:

- **Options analysis** (common case): scope & givens · existing prior art · options
  (each with approach, tradeoffs, standards fit, evidence tags) · recommendation
  (if requested) · open questions / unverified assumptions.
- **ADR** — a single decision to record: context, decision, alternatives, both
  directions of consequence.
- **TRE research story** — feeds Jira: problem statement, findings, proposed
  approach, acceptance criteria, links to verified sources.

## Exit

- When the task turns into writing code, invoke `sb-implement` first — it loads the
  universal coding base and the matching domain standards before the first edit.
.claude/skills/sb-review/SKILL.md:
---
name: sb-review
description: "Begin the code-review phase in a Sandbox sandbox workspace. Use BEFORE reviewing any diff, branch, or PR — self-reviewing your own branch before creating a PR, or reviewing someone else's PR. Loads the standards and workspace decisions the diff must be judged against."
---

# sb-review — enter the code-review phase

Run these steps before reading the first line of the diff. A review without the
active standards in context degrades to taste — the checklist has to load first.

1. **Read the "Standards routing" block** in the workspace `CLAUDE.md`.
2. **Map the diff to domains:** list the files the diff touches and match them
   against each Active row's "Loads on" patterns. Load every matching
   `sb-*-standard` skill. The inline anti-pattern one-liners in each standard
   are your review checklist; open a linked `ap-*.md` war story only when you
   suspect the diff hits it — not preemptively.
3. **Load the universal base** — `sb-comments-standard` (the comment rubric) and
   `sb-engineering-standard` (the cross-cutting architectural constraints: fit,
   additive/reversible change, budgets, PR sizing). Both apply to every review,
   regardless of which files the diff touches.
4. **Read the workspace notes** in `.sandbox/notes/`: every `decision` and
   `contract` note (skip `status: superseded`). A diff that violates a
   `decision` note is itself a review finding — cite the note in the finding.

   > **Precedence (standard vs. author's framing):** When a standard rule conflicts with
   > how the diff justifies itself — a PR description, an "intentional" inline comment, a
   > minimal-change rationale — weight the finding by the standard's own severity, not by
   > how deliberate the change reads:
   > - **Invariant** (a must-never rule `sandbox skills check` enforces): a blocking
   >   finding — cite the rule and request the change; the author's framing does not waive it.
   > - **Rule** (a normal STANDARD.md rule): raise it as a finding and let the author
   >   respond — surface it, do not drop it because the diff looks deliberate.
   > - **Nit** (a style / anti-pattern one-liner): note it as optional / low-severity; no block.
5. **Run the review process:**
   - Reviewing your own branch before a PR → use
     `superpowers:requesting-code-review`.
   - Reviewing someone else's PR → use your PR-review skill.
   - Neither installed → say so once and review directly against the loaded
     checklists.

## Capture as you go

When a review nit reveals a pattern worth codifying that no active standard
covers, write a `decision` note to `.sandbox/notes/` **at that moment** — one
note per file, `NNN-<type>-<slug>.md` (next free `NNN`), frontmatter:

```yaml
---
type: decision
phase: review
author: main
refs: [<files / standard domain it concerns>]
status: open
---
```

`sandbox down` will offer to graduate it into `docs/standards/`.

If the workspace `CLAUDE.md` has no "Standards routing" block (not a
sandbox-initialized workspace), load `sb-comments-standard` +
`sb-engineering-standard` only and review against them.
.claude/skills/sb-test/SKILL.md:
---
name: sb-test
description: "Begin the test phase in a sandbox workspace. Use when running or writing tests — after an implementation lands, before review or a PR, or when the user asks to verify a change with the test suite."
---

# sb-test — enter the test phase

- **Step 0 — scope the run.** From the change at hand (the diff, or the task if nothing
  is edited yet), identify which services are affected, then read the workspace
  `CLAUDE.md` "Standards routing" block to see which archetypes those services belong
  to. When in doubt, `.sandbox/service-map.md` maps repos to services.
- Do **not** load the code standards yourself — the tester agents carry the pointer to
  the standard that governs test code; this phase's main-agent job is dispatch and
  interpretation.
- **Spawn the matching `sb-tester-<archetype>` agent(s)** (generated into
  `.claude/agents/`) — one per archetype whose services the change touches; spawn them
  in parallel when there is more than one. Each agent carries its services' exact test
  commands, may edit **test files only**, and returns per-service pass/fail, failing
  assertions with suspected causes, and open questions.
- **Fallback** (a workspace generated before tester agents existed, or a service with
  no tester): run the tests inline under the same rules — the test command comes from
  services.yaml via `.sandbox/service-map.md` or the repo's `package.json`; edit only
  test files; never "fix" application source in this phase.
- Relay the results per service, then put the testers' OPEN QUESTIONS / AMBIGUITIES to
  the user (AskUserQuestion) and let them resolve those **before** proposing fixes.
- Fixing a failure is the implement phase: invoke `sb-implement` first (it loads the
  universal base and the matching domain standards), and capture an abandoned approach
  or a settled decision as a `.sandbox/notes/` note at the moment it happens.

# yaml-language-server: $schema=https://raw.githubusercontent.com/jbbz-sandbox/sandbox/main/infra/schemas/workspace.schema.json
# AUTO-GENERATED — durable source of truth for workspace inputs.
# Tool:    sandbox init-workspace
# Source:  src/commands/init_workspace.ts :: _write_workspace_config
# Edit:    Hand-edit `feature`, `repos`, `services`, `jira_id`, `task`,
#          `test_path`, `description`, `labels`, or `starting_prompt` below; rerun
#          `sandbox init-workspace` to propagate changes into
#          CLAUDE.md / .env / docker-compose.yml / .sandbox/*.
#          Adding/removing a repo here reconciles git worktrees on rerun;
#          removing a repo with uncommitted edits needs `--force`.
#          Optional `standards_override: {add: [...], remove: [...]}` tunes

**Phase entry:** invoke `sb-research` when exploring or planning; invoke `sb-implement` BEFORE your first code edit — it loads the universal base (`ponytail` + `sb-comments-standard`) and the Active rows matching the files you edit; invoke `sb-test` to run or write tests; invoke `sb-review` BEFORE reviewing any diff or PR; invoke `sb-pr` to finish the branch and create the PR.

> Sessions must start at the **workspace root** (this directory) — the sb-* skills, agents, and hooks live in `.claude/` here and are not found from inside a repo worktree. `sandbox skills check` verifies the skills are current with the sandbox repo.

**By phase:**

| Phase | Entry skill | Load |
|-------|-------------|------|
| research / planning | `sb-research` | nothing — spawns the read-only `sb-researcher` agent |
| implementing | `sb-implement` | universal base + rows matching the files you edit |
| testing | `sb-test` | nothing — spawns the matching `sb-tester-<archetype>` agent(s) |
| review | `sb-review` | the standards covering files in the diff |
| PR / finishing | `sb-pr` | nothing — runs the pre-PR gate, then `sb-review` |

## Notes

Working notes for this feature live in [.sandbox/notes/](.sandbox/notes/) — one note per file, `NNN-<type>-<slug>.md`. Types: `finding` (research output), `decision` (settled choices — binding), `attempt` (tried-and-failed approaches), `handoff` (session/phase transition state), `contract` (cross-repo interface changes). Conventions: docs/notes-conventions.md in the sandbox repo.

List and read the relevant notes before starting work; skip `status: superseded` notes. `decision` notes override task-level instincts (minimal-change, "the prompt didn't mention it") — if one conflicts with the task as given, raise the conflict to the user instead of silently picking a side.
